Given series:
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} u_n = \frac{x}{1\cdot 2} + \frac{x^2}{2\cdot 3} + \frac{x^3}{3\cdot 4} + \dots + \frac{x^n}{n(n+1)} + \dots$$

The $n$-th term of the series is:
$$u_n = \frac{x^n}{n(n+1)}$$

The $(n+1)$-th term is:
$$u_{n+1} = \frac{x^{n+1}}{(n+1)(n+2)}$$

Applying D'Alembert's Ratio Test:
$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \frac{u_n}{u_{n+1}} \right| = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \frac{x^n}{n(n+1)} 	imes \frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{x^{n+1}} \right| = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \frac{1}{x}  rac{n+2}{n} \right| = \frac{1}{x}$$

By ratio test:
- Series converges if $\frac{1}{x} > 1 ightarrow |x| < 1$
- Series diverges if $\frac{1}{x} < 1 ightarrow |x| > 1$

For $x = 1$:
$$u_n = \frac{1}{n(n+1)} 	hickapprox  rac{1}{n^2}$$ 
By $p$-series test ($p = 2 > 1$), the series converges at $x = 1$.

For $x = -1$:
The series becomes alternating and absolutely converges.

Thus, the series is convergent for $-1 ≤ x ≤ 1$.
proTip: Always test the end points ($x = \pm 1$) explicitly when the ratio test yields a limit of 1.
